messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Carlos

Carlos had been a parole officer for twenty-three years when the call came in about a violation in the North End district. He was fifty-four, meticulous in his work, known among his colleagues for his fairness and his refusal to cut corners. He had built a reputation on the principle that men deserved a second chance if they showed they were serious about change. On that October afternoon in 2019, he was following up on a parolee who had missed three consecutive check-ins. The man lived in a basement apartment on Ashland Avenue. Carlos knocked, identified himself, and waited. When the door opened a crack, he saw the chain still fastened, a pair of eyes in shadow. He explained that he needed to conduct a welfare check. The man said he was fine, asked him to come back later. Carlos, professional and patient, explained that this was routine, that it would only take a few minutes. He heard footsteps retreating into the apartment. Then silence.

That silence stretched. Carlos waited, his hand resting on the frame. The door was still chained. He called out once more, identifying himself again. No response. He was reaching for his radio to request a supervisor when the door exploded inward—the chain snapped, the frame splintered—and three officers in tactical gear poured through, shouting commands. Carlos had not called for backup. He understood, in the fractured seconds that followed, that this was not his case anymore. He stepped back, raising his hands to show he was one of them. But the officers had momentum and adrenaline. One of them, a sergeant he did not recognize, drove him hard against the wall. Carlos felt his ribs compress, his breath cut short. He heard himself say, "I'm parole—I'm parole," but his voice was thin, lost in the shouting. The sergeant's forearm was across his throat. Carlos tried to turn his head, tried to show his badge, but the pressure intensified. His vision narrowed. He remembered thinking, with a clarity that felt almost abstract, that he might lose consciousness. Then, as abruptly as it began, it stopped. The sergeant released him. The officers moved past him into the apartment. Carlos stood against the wall, gasping, his hand at his neck, watching them work.

The aftermath was procedural and hollow. Internal Affairs reviewed the incident. The sergeant claimed Carlos had not clearly identified himself. Carlos's own statement was taken, filed, and eventually closed with a finding of "insufficient evidence of misconduct." No discipline. No apology. The department moved on. But Carlos could not. What had happened to him—the betrayal of it, the sheer injustice—had lodged itself in a place he could not reach or reason with. He had spent his career inside the system, trusting it, serving it. The officers who had pinned him to the wall were his colleagues. The institution that should have protected him had decided, in effect, that nothing had happened worth correcting. He was certain now that the system he served was not what he had believed it to be, that the men and women who wore the badge could turn on you without warning, and that no one would answer for it.

In the months that followed, Carlos began to notice how the trauma had fractured his memory of the event itself. He could recall the knock on the door, the chain, the silence—but the moment of impact remained jagged and incomplete, as though his mind had shattered it into pieces he could not fit back together. When he tried to reconstruct it, the sequence slipped away from him. He found himself pushing the memory down before it could fully form, a protective reflex that had become automatic. What remained was a sense of unreality, a feeling that the violence could not have been as severe as his body insisted it had been. Surely he was exaggerating. Surely he had misunderstood what was happening. But his neck still bore faint bruising weeks later, and his ribs ached when he breathed deeply. The contradiction between what had happened and his mind's refusal to hold it whole left him in a state of constant doubt.

That doubt fed into everything. When people misbehaved—a parolee lying during a check-in, a colleague dismissing his concerns—Carlos felt a surge of anger and betrayal that seemed disproportionate to the moment. His heart would race, and he would find himself gripping the edge of his desk, certain that the world was fundamentally corrupt, that trust was a fool's game. The injustice of what had been done to him, and the institutional silence that had followed, had become the lens through which he saw all moral failure. Every small violation felt like proof of the larger truth: that power was unaccountable, that the innocent could be crushed without consequence, that the systems meant to protect people were rotten from within.

At home, his hypervigilance had become the texture of his days. Carlos sat in the living room with his wife, María, and found his eyes moving constantly to the windows, the hallway, the space behind the kitchen door. Unusual silence—the absence of traffic noise, of neighbors, of the ambient hum of the city—made his stomach tighten. He was certain something dangerous was about to happen. His heart would begin to race, and he would stand, moving to check the locks, to look outside. María would ask him what was wrong, and he could not explain it in a way that made sense. He was jumpy, startled by her touch, by the phone ringing, by the ordinary sounds of their house. The threat felt constant and invisible, and the only way to manage it was to remain alert, to scan, to anticipate. His mind, trying to protect him, had become his jailer.

What brought him finally to seek help was a moment of clarity that felt like a crack in the wall he had built around himself. María had asked him, quietly, if he was still there with her, or if the man she had married had been replaced by someone she no longer recognized. He could not answer. He knew that the hypervigilance, the rage, the fragmented memory—all of it was destroying the life he had worked so carefully to build. He was terrified that if he did not find a way to make sense of what had happened to him, he would lose everything that mattered. And yet he was equally afraid that examining the trauma directly would confirm what he most feared: that the world was as broken as he now believed it to be, and that he had been betrayed by the very institution that had been supposed to define him.
